The odd one out is (b) Mediterranean forests.

The chapter lists the forest types of India as evergreen, deciduous, thorny and shrub-type, coastal (mangrove or Sunderbans) and the three Himalayan types. Mangrove forests, thorny bush-type vegetation and equatorial or evergreen forests are therefore all found in India; Mediterranean forests are not among the types the chapter names.

The odd one out is (d) Lion.

The chapter names the anaconda among the animals of the swampy Pantanal, the macaw among the major birds of Brazil, and the golden lion tamarin among the species shown on its wildlife map. The lion belongs to India — the chapter says India is the only country in the world where both tigers and lions are found.

The odd one out is (c) Orchid.

Deodar is named among the coniferous trees of the Indian Himalayas, banyan among the trees of India's deciduous forests, and anjan is an Indian thorny-forest tree. Orchids are named in this chapter as part of the flora of BRAZIL, in the list of trees found there along with Pau Brasil, rubber, mahogany and rosewood.
